hypotheses.title: Static signature bypasses image hash validation entirely
hypotheses.description: When the top bit of the signature flag is set (`signatureFlag & 0x80 == 0x80`), `signatureValidation` returns `(true, opHash)` without ever calling `_isValidImage`. The only checks are that the static signature has not expired and that the stored address is either zero or equals `msg.sender`. If `addr == address(0)` (i.e. no static signature was ever set for this opHash), the caller check is skipped and the function returns valid. This means any caller can pass a signature whose first byte has the high bit set and, provided the (unset) static signature timestamp is `0 <= block.timestamp` — which is always true since `_getStaticSignature` returns `0` for unset hashes — the validation succeeds.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker crafts a payload and a signature whose first byte is `0x80` (or any byte with bit 7 set). 2) Attacker calls `execute(payload, signature)` on the wallet. 3) `signatureValidation` reads the flag, computes `opHash`, calls `_getStaticSignature(opHash)` which returns `(address(0), 0)`. 4) `timestamp <= block.timestamp` is `0 <= now` → true, so no revert. 5) `addr == address(0)` so the caller check is skipped. 6) Returns `(true, opHash)`. 7) `_execute` runs the attacker's calls.
hypotheses.impact: Complete authentication bypass — any external actor can execute arbitrary calls on any wallet, draining all funds and assets.
hypotheses.recommendation: Revert when `addr == address(0)` (no static signature set) and require `timestamp > block.timestamp` (i.e. an actual expiry was set), rather than treating an unset signature as valid.

hypotheses.title: Static signature expiry check inverted allows expired signatures
hypotheses.description: The check `if (timestamp <= block.timestamp) revert InvalidStaticSignatureExpired(...)` reverts when the timestamp is in the past, which is the correct direction for an expiry — but combined with the unset case (`timestamp == 0`), it means an unset static signature is treated as "not expired" and passes. More importantly, the semantics are inverted relative to the error name: a signature with `timestamp == 0` (never set) is accepted, and a signature with a future timestamp is accepted, but a signature with a past timestamp is rejected. The real flaw is that the "unset" case is indistinguishable from "valid forever" and is accepted.
hypotheses.attackPath: Same as the previous finding — an attacker supplies a signature with the high bit set and no static signature has been configured for the resulting opHash, so `timestamp == 0` passes the check and `addr == address(0)` skips the caller check.
hypotheses.impact: Authentication bypass leading to arbitrary call execution and loss of all wallet funds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require `timestamp != 0` and `timestamp > block.timestamp` before accepting a static signature; treat unset as invalid.

hypotheses.title: Cumulative usage limit double-counts within same payload
hypotheses.description: When a cumulative rule is validated, the code searches `newUsageLimits` for an existing entry with the same `usageHash`. If found, it uses `usageLimit.usageAmount` as `previousUsage`. However, the search loop breaks on the first slot with `usageHash == bytes32(0)` (initializing a new entry) before checking later slots. Since `newUsageLimits` is pre-sized to `usageLimits.length + permission.rules.length` and initialized with zeros, the first empty slot is always found before any previously-added entry from a prior call in the same payload. This means each call in the same payload re-reads from storage instead of accumulating the in-memory value, so the cumulative limit is not enforced across multiple calls in one payload.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker obtains a session with a cumulative usage limit rule (e.g., max 100 tokens per session). 2) Attacker crafts a payload with N calls, each transferring 100 tokens to the same target. 3) Each call's `validatePermission` reads `previousUsage` from storage (still 0) rather than the in-memory accumulated value, so each call passes the limit check. 4) The final `incrementUsageLimit` call writes only the last call's value (100) to storage. 5) Attacker drains N×100 tokens while the session limit records only 100.
hypotheses.impact: Session usage limits are bypassed; attacker can drain unlimited funds from the wallet within a single payload despite configured cumulative limits.
hypotheses.recommendation: Search the entire `newUsageLimits` array for a matching `usageHash` before falling back to the first empty slot; do not break on the first zero slot.

hypotheses.title: Session signature replay across wallets via missing wallet binding in call hash
hypotheses.description: The per-call hash signed by session signers is computed from `block.chainid`, `payload.space`, `payload.nonce`, `callIdx`, and the call hash — but it does NOT include the wallet address (`address(this)`). The wallet address is only bound into the outer EIP-712 domain via `Payload.hash`, which is used for the top-level signature, not for the session signer's per-call signature. As a result, the exact same `(space, nonce, callIdx, call)` tuple produces the same `callHash` on every wallet that shares the same chainId, so a session signer's signature over a call is valid on any wallet whose session configuration contains that signer.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes a session signer's signed call for wallet A (e.g. via mempool or by being a co-signer). 2) Attacker constructs an identical payload (same space, nonce, callIdx, call data) targeting wallet B, where the same session signer is also authorized. 3) Attacker submits the payload to wallet B with the same session signature. 4) `recoverSignature` recovers the same session signer and `_validateExplicitCall`/`_validateImplicitCall` accept it because the signer is authorized on wallet B. 5) The call executes on wallet B without the session signer's consent for that wallet.
hypotheses.impact: Unauthorized execution of calls on any wallet sharing a session signer; potential loss of funds or asset transfers from victim wallets.
hypotheses.recommendation: Include `address(this)` (the wallet) in `hashCallWithReplayProtection` so the session signer's signature is bound to a specific wallet.

hypotheses.title: SessionManager bans self-calls but ExplicitSessionManager allows incrementUsageLimit self-call
hypotheses.description: `recoverSapientSignature` rejects any call where `call.to == wallet` with `InvalidSelfCall`. However, `ExplicitSessionManager._validateExplicitCall` explicitly permits a call to `address(this)` (the wallet) when `callIdx == 0` for `incrementUsageLimit`, and `_validateLimitUsageIncrement` requires the first call to be exactly that self-call when usage limits are used. This is a contradiction: any explicit session that uses usage limits will always revert in `recoverSapientSignature` because the required first call targets the wallet itself.
hypotheses.attackPath: Not an external attack per se, but any user attempting to use explicit sessions with usage limits will find their transactions always revert, effectively bricking that feature. An attacker cannot directly exploit it, but it constitutes a liveness failure for a documented feature.
hypotheses.impact: Explicit sessions with usage limits are unusable; users cannot execute permitted calls, and any funds/operations gated behind such sessions are frozen.
hypotheses.recommendation: Allow the specific `incrementUsageLimit` self-call in `recoverSapientSignature` (or move the self-call ban to `_validateExplicitCall` with the same exception).

hypotheses.title: Session usage limits bypassed via incrementUsageLimit self-call
hypotheses.description: `incrementUsageLimit` is externally callable and only checks that the new `usageAmount` is not less than the current stored value (`limits[i].usageAmount < getLimitUsage(...)` reverts). Any caller can set the stored usage to an arbitrarily large value, which permanently inflates the "previous usage" used by `validatePermission` for cumulative rules. Because `_validateLimitUsageIncrement` only verifies that the first call's calldata matches the expected increment derived from the payload's own computed limits, a session signer can craft a payload whose first call is `incrementUsageLimit` with a huge `usageAmount` for the cumulative usage hash, then subsequent calls in the same payload will see `previousUsage` = huge value and the cumulative comparison will pass trivially (or the session's cumulative budget is exhausted, but the attacker controls the value). More critically, the attacker can pre-inflate the stored usage to `type(uint256).max` so that any later cumulative check overflows/reverts or is effectively disabled depending on the rule direction.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker obtains a session signature for a payload. 2) Attacker crafts the first call as `incrementUsageLimit` with `usageAmount = type(uint256).max` for the cumulative usage hash of a rule they want to bypass. 3) `_validateLimitUsageIncrement` builds the expected limits from the payload's own computed `sessionUsageLimits`, which the attacker also controls via the crafted call data, so the hash matches. 4) The stored usage is set to max, and subsequent cumulative checks in the same or later payloads use this inflated `previousUsage`, allowing the attacker to bypass the intended cumulative cap (or cause the session to be permanently unusable, griefing the wallet owner).
hypotheses.impact: Session cumulative spending limits can be bypassed or permanently bricked, allowing a session signer to spend beyond the intended cap or DoS the wallet's session functionality.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict `incrementUsageLimit` to `onlySelf` (i.e., only callable via the wallet's own execution path) and/or validate that the increment matches the exact expected delta computed from the payload rather than trusting caller-supplied `usageAmount`.

hypotheses.title: Session signature replay across chains when noChainId flag is set
hypotheses.description: When `payload.noChainId` is true, the per-call hash uses `0` instead of `block.chainid`. Combined with the missing wallet binding (see above), a session signer's signature over a call is valid on every chain and every wallet that authorizes that signer. The `noChainId` flag is attacker-controllable via the signature flag byte in `BaseSig.recover` (`_payload.noChainId = signatureFlag & 0x02 == 0x02`), so an attacker can force the no-chain-id variant even if the signer intended a chain-bound signature.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker obtains a session signer's signature over a call (or is a session signer themselves). 2) Attacker crafts a payload with the `noChainId` bit set in the signature flag. 3) Attacker replays the same signed call on a different chain where the same session signer is authorized. 4) The call hash matches because chainId is forced to 0, and the session signer is accepted. 5) The call executes on the target chain.
hypotheses.impact: Cross-chain replay of session-authorized calls; unauthorized asset transfers or state changes on other chains.
hypotheses.recommendation: Bind the session signer's per-call hash to the actual chainId regardless of the `noChainId` flag, or require the signer to explicitly opt into chain-agnostic signatures with a distinct domain.

hypotheses.title: Cross-function reentrancy via selfExecute during execute() callbacks
hypotheses.description: `selfExecute` is guarded by `onlySelf` (msg.sender == address(this)), but during `_execute` the wallet performs arbitrary external calls. If one of those calls targets the wallet itself (e.g., a call to `selfExecute` with a crafted payload), the `onlySelf` check passes because `msg.sender` is the wallet. `selfExecute` is NOT protected by `nonReentrant` (only `execute` and `executeUserOp` are), so a reentrant `selfExecute` can run a second payload while the first is still in flight. This allows the attacker to execute a second payload that observes and manipulates mid-flight state (nonce already consumed, usage limits not yet incremented).
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker crafts payload A with a call to the wallet's own `selfExecute` selector, passing payload B as calldata. 2) `execute(A)` consumes nonce, validates signature, enters `_execute`. 3) The call to `selfExecute(B)` succeeds because `msg.sender == address(this)`. 4) `selfExecute(B)` runs payload B, which can read stale usage limits or perform additional calls that the original signature did not authorize. 5) Payload B's calls execute before payload A's remaining calls, breaking the intended ordering.
hypotheses.impact: An attacker who controls a session signer can execute arbitrary additional calls beyond what was signed, bypassing session permissions and usage limits — loss of funds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `nonReentrant` to `selfExecute`, or check the reentrancy status inside `selfExecute` before proceeding.

hypotheses.title: session callHash uses block.chainid but noChainId flag can be set to 0 by attacker
hypotheses.description: `hashCallWithReplayProtection` includes `payload.noChainId ? 0 : block.chainid`. `payload.noChainId` is fully attacker-controlled inside the payload passed to `recoverSapientSignature`. An attacker can craft a session signature over a payload with `noChainId = true` (chainid omitted), and the wallet's `recoverSapientSignature` will accept it regardless of current chain. Since `noChainId` is not part of the hash commitment that the identity signer approves (the identity signer signs `hashCallWithReplayProtection` which uses the flag but the flag itself is not bound to a trusted value — an attacker only needs the session key's signature over a payload with noChainId=true). The same signed payload can then be replayed on every chain where the wallet exists at the same address.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker obtains a valid session signature over a payload with `noChainId = true`. 2) Replays the identical payload on another chain where the wallet is deployed at the same address and the nonce hasn't been consumed. 3) Wallet executes calls the session signer intended for one chain.
hypotheses.impact: Cross-chain replay of session-authorized calls, including fund transfers.
hypotheses.recommendation: Do not let the session payload decide `noChainId`; force `noChainId = false` in SessionManager.recoverSapientSignature, or bind the flag inside the identity-signer-controlled configuration.

hypotheses.title: Static signature path accepts caller-independent authorization with expired/zero semantics
hypotheses.description: When the top bit (0x80) of the signature flag is set, `signatureValidation` treats the transaction as authorized purely based on `_getStaticSignature(opHash)`. It reverts only when `timestamp <= block.timestamp` (i.e., expiry is `<= now`), and it permits `addr == address(0)` to bypass the caller check entirely. A wallet that has never set a static signature for that opHash has `timestamp == 0`, so the revert fires — but any party who knows an opHash whose stored static signature has `timestamp == 0` and `addr == address(0)` will hit the revert, while if the entry exists with a nonzero future timestamp and `addr == address(0)`, the caller check is skipped and any caller (including the ERC-4337 EntryPoint, or anyone via `execute`) passes. The check `addr != address(0)` gating wrong-caller revert means a static signature registered with `address(0)` is universally callable.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Wallet (or a buggy off-chain flow) writes a static signature entry via `setStaticSignature(hash, address(0), futureTs)` — which is allowed because only `onlySelf` gates it. 2) Anyone crafts a payload whose `Payload.hash()` equals `hash`. 3) Calls `execute(payload, signature)` with first byte `0x80`. 4) `timestamp > block.timestamp` true, `addr == address(0)` so caller check is skipped. 5) `isValid = true` returned, `_execute` runs arbitrary calls.
hypotheses.impact: Arbitrary execution of privileged wallet calls including `updateImageHash`, `updateImplementation`, `addHook`, `setStaticSignature`, `updateImplementation` — full wallet takeover / loss of all funds. Also, since `execute` is `external payable` and unauthenticated other than this check, third parties can drain the wallet.
hypotheses.recommendation: Reject `_address == address(0)` in `_setStaticSignature`, and revert when the stored entry is missing (timestamp == 0) rather than relying on `<= block.timestamp`; additionally require `msg.sender == entrypoint` (or explicitly authorize callers) on the static path.

hypotheses.title: Simulator.simulate has no access control and can trigger arbitrary delegatecalls
hypotheses.description: `simulate` is fully external with no `onlySelf`, no `nonReentrant`, no `msg.sender` restriction, and no nonce consumption. Any caller can pass arbitrary `Payload.Call[]` and cause the `Simulator` contract itself to execute `delegateCall` to attacker-chosen targets with attacker-chosen calldata (via the `IDelegatedExtension.handleSequenceDelegateCall` path). Because it's `delegatecall` in the Simulator's context, an attacker can overwrite Simulator storage (including inherited `IMAGE_HASH_KEY`-style slots, `Storage`-keyed values, and `Implementation` storage) or invoke other privileged hooks.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deploys or uses an existing target whose `handleSequenceDelegateCall` performs `sstore` on arbitrary slots or calls privileged functions in the Simulator's context. 2) Calls `Simulator.simulate(calls)` with `delegateCall = true`, `to = attackerContract`. 3) Simulator delegatecalls into attacker code, which writes to Simulator storage or re-enters Simulator's `selfExecute`-like paths.
hypotheses.impact: Storage corruption of the Simulator module, potential takeover of the Simulator contract itself (which sometimes is delegated from a wallet in the Sequence architecture), and abuse as an on-chain arbitrary-delegatecall primitive for any caller.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict `simulate` to `msg.sender == address(this)` (or an explicit opt-in flag) and/or disallow `delegateCall` in the simulation path; add `nonReentrant`.

hypotheses.title: Guest fallback decodes arbitrary calldata and executes calls unconditionally
hypotheses.description: `Guest`'s `fallback()` decodes `msg.data` into a `Payload.Decoded` and executes the contained calls with no signature validation whatsoever (no `signatureValidation`, no `onlySelf`, no nonce). Any external actor can call the Guest with a crafted payload and cause it to make arbitrary `call`s (with `value` from its own balance, `gasLimit`, and `behaviorOnError`) — the only restriction is that `delegateCall` is banned. The docstring does not indicate `Guest` is a write-protected module, but in this codebase it is a deployed contract taking calls from the public.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker crafts a payload with calls that transfer any ERC20/ETH the Guest holds, or interact with any protocol the Guest is trusted with. 2) Calls `Guest.fallback()` with that payload. 3) `_dispatchGuest` loops and performs the calls.
hypotheses.impact: If the Guest holds funds or is trusted (e.g., addresses an integration relies on), any external actor drains it or makes it perform arbitrary actions attributed to its address.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require a valid signature (reuse `BaseAuth.signatureValidation` against an owner image) or restrict the Guest fallback to `msg.sender == address(this)`/known modules.

hypotheses.title: Nonce consumption in Estimator allows replay of estimate
hypotheses.description: The `estimate` function calls `_consumeNonce(decoded.space, readNonce(decoded.space))`, which reads the current nonce and consumes it (increments it). This means that calling `estimate` advances the nonce, which could interfere with the actual execution of the payload. If a user calls `estimate` and then tries to execute the same payload, the nonce will have already been incremented, causing the execution to fail with `BadNonce`. This is a denial of service for the user, as they cannot estimate and then execute the same payload.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) User calls `estimate` with a payload. 2) The nonce is incremented. 3) User calls `execute` with the same payload. 4) The nonce check fails because the nonce was already consumed by `estimate`. 5) The user's transaction reverts.
hypotheses.impact: Users cannot estimate gas and then execute the same payload; they must use a different nonce or re-sign the payload, causing inconvenience and potential loss of gas.
hypotheses.recommendation: Do not consume the nonce in `estimate`; use a read-only nonce check or simulate without state changes.

hypotheses.title: Reentrancy via ERC-1155/777/721 hooks during execute() callbacks
hypotheses.description: The `_execute` loop performs arbitrary external calls (`LibOptim.call`) to attacker-controlled contracts before the nonReentrant guard is released, but the guard only protects the top-level `execute`/`selfExecute` entrypoints. Because `Hooks.sol` exposes `onERC1155Received`, `onERC1155BatchReceived`, `onERC721Received`, `tokensReceived`, and `tokenReceived` as public entrypoints that are NOT gated by `nonReentrant`, an attacker can re-enter the wallet through these hooks while a call is in flight. The hooks themselves are no-ops, but the wallet's `fallback()` in `Hooks.sol` will delegatecall any registered hook implementation, and more importantly the wallet's `execute`/`selfExecute` are reachable via `selfExecute` (onlySelf) or via the ERC-4337 `executeUserOp` path — but the critical issue is that the reentrancy guard is stored in a single slot and the hook entrypoints do not check it, so any state that is mid-update (e.g., nonce already consumed, usage limits not yet written) can be observed and manipulated.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker crafts a payload where one of the calls targets a malicious ERC-1155/777/721 token contract. 2) During `LibOptim.call`, the token invokes `onERC1155Received` (or `tokensReceived`) on the wallet. 3) The hook is a no-op, but the attacker can chain this with a second call in the same payload that reads stale state (e.g., `readNonce`, `getLimitUsage`) or with a cross-contract call to `SessionManager.recoverSapientSignature` which reads `getLimitUsage` before the increment call has executed. 4) Because `_consumeNonce` writes the nonce before the calls execute, but usage-limit increments are only applied by the first call in the payload, a reentrant read of `getLimitUsage` during a later call sees the pre-increment value, allowing the attacker to bypass cumulative limits.
hypotheses.impact: Session usage limits (cumulative value limits, cumulative parameter rules) can be bypassed, allowing a session signer to spend more than the configured limit — loss of funds from the wallet.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `nonReentrant` to all hook entrypoints in `Hooks.sol`, or move the reentrancy guard to a shared modifier that also covers the hook callbacks.

hypotheses.title: ERC-4337 executeUserOp reentrancy via selfExecute bypasses nonReentrant
hypotheses.description: `executeUserOp` is `nonReentrant` and calls `this.selfExecute(_payload)`. `selfExecute` is `onlySelf` but NOT `nonReentrant`. Because `executeUserOp` sets the reentrancy status to `_ENTERED` and then calls `selfExecute` via `this.` (an external call), the `selfExecute` function itself does not check the guard. If during `selfExecute`'s `_execute` loop an external call re-enters `executeUserOp` (via the EntryPoint) or `selfExecute` directly, the guard on `executeUserOp` will block the former but not the latter. The attacker can therefore re-enter `selfExecute` directly from a callback.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker submits a UserOperation whose payload contains a call to a malicious contract. 2) EntryPoint calls `executeUserOp`, which sets `_ENTERED` and calls `selfExecute`. 3) During `_execute`, the malicious contract calls `wallet.selfExecute(payloadB)` — `msg.sender` is the wallet (because the malicious contract was called by the wallet, and it calls back into the wallet), so `onlySelf` passes. 4) Payload B executes while payload A is mid-flight.
hypotheses.impact: Bypass of session permissions and usage limits; arbitrary additional calls executed under a single signed payload.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `nonReentrant` to `selfExecute` so the guard is enforced on the inner entrypoint as well.

hypotheses.title: Unbounded loop in Recovery.queuePayload allows griefing of queued payloads
hypotheses.description: `queuedPayloadHashes[_wallet][_signer]` is an unbounded array that grows by one entry per successful `queuePayload` call. Any external actor who can produce a valid signature for a given `_signer` (e.g. a legitimate recovery signer, or a signer whose key is compromised/leaked) can push arbitrarily many distinct payload hashes. There is no removal path, so the array can grow without bound, and any consumer that iterates over `totalQueuedPayloads` (or off-chain tooling that reads the full array) will eventually run out of gas or become unusable.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker obtains a valid signature for `_signer` over many distinct payloads (or is the legitimate signer). 2) Attacker calls `queuePayload(_wallet, _signer, payload_i, sig_i)` repeatedly with unique payloads. 3) Each call appends to `queuedPayloadHashes[_wallet][_signer]` and cannot be undone. 4) The array grows unbounded, making any on-chain or off-chain enumeration of queued payloads prohibitively expensive.
hypotheses.impact: Recovery queue for a wallet/signer becomes effectively unusable; off-chain recovery tooling that enumerates queued payloads will fail, and any future on-chain logic that iterates the array will revert with out-of-gas, freezing the recovery flow.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add a bounded queue with explicit removal/expiry, or store only the latest timestamp per payload hash and avoid an unbounded append-only array.

hypotheses.title: Static signature replay without nonce/expiry window, callable by any caller
hypotheses.description: When the top bit of the signature flag is set (0x80), any caller who possesses a valid static signature for an opHash can call execute() with that exact payload indefinitely as long as `_timestamp > block.timestamp`. The static signature is bound only to `opHash` and an optional caller address, but the underlying `opHash` is computed from a payload whose nonce is *consumed* in Calls.execute before signatureValidation — yet the static path returns `(true, opHash)` without comparing against the caller-controlled nonce in any signature scheme (the nonce values in the payload are irrelevant because the attacker can craft any payload that hashes the same? No—opHash changes with nonce). The critical issue: when `addr == address(0)` (which is explicitly allowed by the check `if (addr != address(0) && addr != msg.sender)`), any caller may replay the exact same signed payload. Because the static signature is set once and never invalidated, and the nonce in the payload is checked against the wallet's current nonce (which the attacker can always match by choosing the correct payload), the same signed payload cannot actually be replayed after the nonce increments — but the static signature path also does NOT verify the payload's calls relate to the timestamp at all. The real bug is that the static signature is keyed on `opHash`, which is derived from `msg.sender`-independent fields; once set, the entry can be reused forever (until expiry) with the same payload, but since nonce increments this is self-limiting. However, note that `setStaticSignature` allows setting the expiry in the future, and the static signature bypasses BaseSig entirely, so any caller can submit the same payload again with nonce=N+1? No — the nonce would have to be signed. The stored key is the opHash of a specific nonce. Actually the concrete flaw is: the static signature validation is gated on `addr != address(0) && addr != msg.sender` — meaning if the caller address equals the stored caller it's allowed, but if `addr == address(0)` (which is a valid stored state — see setStaticSignature allowing any address including 0), then there is NO caller binding at all, and combined with the fact that the same opHash can correspond to a selfExecute payload (no nonce consumption) the same static signature can be replayed.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Wallet owner sets a static signature for a selfExecute payload hash (addr=0 for open access). 2) Any external attacker observes the payload/signature and calls execute(payload, signature-with-0x80-flag) before expiry. 3) The static check returns true for any msg.sender, nonce check passes if the payload's nonce is still current (the nonce is consumed, but the attacker picks the payload the signature was made for). For selfExecute-derived static sigs, nonce is never consumed at all, allowing indefinite replay.
hypotheses.impact: Replay of signed operations, including fund transfers, draining the wallet multiple times (or until expiry).
hypotheses.recommendation: Require a non-zero caller binding (reject addr == address(0)) and/or require the static signature to incorporate the wallet's nonce and expire quickly; alternatively remove the open-caller static path.

hypotheses.title: Recovery queue timestamp can be reset by re-queueing after expiry
hypotheses.description: `queuePayload` reverts with `AlreadyQueued` only if `timestampForQueuedPayload[_wallet][_signer][payloadHash] != 0`. Once a payload has been queued and its timestamp is set, it can never be re-queued (good). However, the recovery leaf check in `_recoverBranch` uses `block.timestamp - queuedAt >= requiredDeltaTime` with no upper bound on how old the queue entry is. A signer who queued a payload long ago can still use it indefinitely, and more importantly, if a signer is compromised or removed from the recovery config, any previously queued payload remains valid forever. There is no mechanism to invalidate queued payloads after a config change, so a removed signer's queued payload can still be used to recover the wallet.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) A recovery signer queues a payload while still authorized. 2) The wallet owner updates the recovery configuration to remove that signer (e.g., because the signer is compromised). 3) The removed signer still holds the queued payload and, after `requiredDeltaTime`, submits it. 4) `_recoverBranch` checks only the timestamp mapping, which is never cleared on config change, so the removed signer's payload is accepted and the wallet is recovered to the attacker's control.
hypotheses.impact: A removed/compromised recovery signer can still recover the wallet using a previously queued payload, leading to full wallet takeover and loss of all funds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Invalidate queued payloads when the recovery configuration changes (e.g., store a config epoch and require queued payloads to match the current epoch), or add an expiry window to queued payloads.

hypotheses.title: Estimator.estimate consumes nonce via readNonce instead of actual nonce
hypotheses.description: `_consumeNonce(decoded.space, readNonce(decoded.space))` reads the current nonce and passes it as the expected nonce, so the check `currentNonce != _nonce` always passes and the nonce is incremented. This means calling `estimate` mutates the wallet's nonce state. Since `estimate` is a public function callable by anyone (it's `external payable`), any external actor can call `estimate` on a wallet to advance its nonce, invalidating pending signed payloads.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Victim signs a payload with nonce N and submits it (or has it pending). 2) Attacker calls `Estimator.estimate(payload, sig)` on the wallet with any payload. 3) The nonce is incremented to N+1. 4) Victim's pending payload with nonce N now reverts with BadNonce.
hypotheses.impact: Denial of service / griefing: attacker can invalidate any pending signed transaction by advancing the nonce. If the wallet is a smart account, this can block user operations.
hypotheses.recommendation: `estimate` should not consume the nonce; use a read-only check or skip nonce consumption entirely in estimation.

hypotheses.title: Estimator.estimate consumes nonce logic incorrectly and re-enables replay in shared flow
hypotheses.description: `estimate` calls `_consumeNonce(decoded.space, readNonce(decoded.space))` — reading the current nonce and immediately passing it back, which increments it as a side effect. Estimating a payload advances the on-chain nonce, so the *real* `execute` with the same payload (same nonce) reverts with `BadNonce`. Conversely, because Estimator inherits `BaseAuth`/`Calls` storage layout but is deployed as a standalone module, it shares storage only with itself, so leaving the Estimator at a specific implementation may not directly affect individual wallets — the direct in-scope bug is nonce advancement within the Estimator contract itself, meaning any estimate call from an untrusted party burns "nonces" in the Estimator's own storage.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls `Estimator.estimate(payload, signature)` repeatedly. 2) Each call increments the Estimator's own nonce for `payload.space`. 3) Since the Estimator is reused (its `_isValidImage` is overridden to always return `true`), any other caller cannot rely on nonce semantics in the Estimator.
hypotheses.impact: Denial of service against other users relying on the Estimator's nonce tracking; incorrect gas accounting assumptions if any integrator assumes estimate is side-effect free.
hypotheses.recommendation: Remove `_consumeNonce` from `estimate` (or replace with a read-only check), since estimation must not mutate state.

hypotheses.title: Recovery.queuePayload caller-controlled _wallet allows squatting and DoS on queue
hypotheses.description: `queuePayload` accepts `_wallet` as a free parameter from the caller, and the `isValidSignature` check is performed against that chosen `_wallet`. Nothing ties `_wallet` to `msg.sender` or to any wallet image. Any actor who can produce an ECDSA/ERC1271 signature by some `_signer` over the recovery EIP-712 hash for a target wallet can queue a payload; once queued, `timestampForQueuedPayload[_wallet][_signer][payloadHash]` is set and duplicate queue attempts revert with `AlreadyQueued`. Because the wallet is arbitrary, a malicious queuer can cause a pending payload to be locked/used (or its slot consumed) in a way that interferes with legitimate recovery timing.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker learns or guesses a payload for a target wallet, or uses a signer they control. 2) Calls `queuePayload(targetWallet, attackerSigner, payload, sig)` — `isValidSignature` passes because `_signer` is attacker-controlled and the signature is over the recovery hash for `targetWallet`. 3) Now `timestampForQueuedPayload[targetWallet][attackerSigner][payloadHash]` is nonzero, blocking any legitimate queue attempt for the same `payloadHash` and starting a recovery timer under attacker influence.
hypotheses.impact: DoS/griefing of the recovery flow; potential to trigger recovery execution timing the legitimate owner cannot control or to make an intended recovery revert as `AlreadyQueued`.
hypotheses.recommendation: Bind `_wallet` to an authorization check (e.g., require `_wallet == msg.sender` or a signature from `_wallet`'s owner over the queue action), and/or namespace queue slots by caller.

hypotheses.title: totalValueUsed not persisted across calls in same payload
hypotheses.description: `sessionUsageLimits.totalValueUsed` is incremented per call and checked against `sessionPermissions.valueLimit`. However, in `SessionManager.recoverSapientSignature`, the `sessionUsageLimits` array is indexed by `limitsIdx` found via a loop that breaks on the first slot with `signer == address(0)`. When a session signer is used for multiple calls, the loop finds the existing entry and returns `limits` (a memory copy). After `_validateExplicitCall` returns the updated `limits`, it is written back to `sessionUsageLimits[limitsIdx]`. This part is correct, but the initial `limits.totalValueUsed` is loaded from storage only once (via `getLimitUsage`). The check `sessionUsageLimits.totalValueUsed > sessionPermissions.valueLimit` uses the accumulated value, so this appears correct. However, the `_validateLimitUsageIncrement` only writes the final total to storage via the increment call, and if the increment call is skipped (e.g., via `onlyFallback` or behavior manipulation), the storage value is never updated, allowing the same value to be spent again in a subsequent payload.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker has a session with valueLimit = 100. 2) Attacker submits a payload spending 100 native tokens. 3) The increment call is included and writes 100 to storage. 4) Attacker submits another payload spending 100 native tokens. 5) The check `totalValueUsed > valueLimit` uses the storage value (100) + new value (100) = 200 > 100, so it reverts. This path is blocked. However, if the attacker can cause the increment call to fail silently (e.g., by making the first call revert with BEHAVIOR_IGNORE_ERROR), the storage is never updated, and the next payload starts from 0 again.
hypotheses.impact: Value limits can be bypassed if the increment call is not executed, allowing repeated spending beyond the configured limit.
hypotheses.recommendation: Ensure the increment call cannot be skipped or bypassed; consider writing usage directly during validation rather than relying on a separate increment call.

hypotheses.title: Session permission index not bound to call index allows permission reuse
hypotheses.description: The `sessionPermission` byte is read from the call signature flags and passed to `_validateExplicitCall` as `permissionIdx`, which indexes into `sessionPermissions.permissions`. The permission index is not bound to the specific call index in the payload — the same permission index can be reused across multiple calls in the same payload, and the same permission can be applied to different calls. Since `_validateExplicitCall` only checks `permissionIdx < sessionPermissions.permissions.length` and validates the permission against the current call, an attacker who controls the payload can pair any permission with any call as long as the permission's target matches the call's `to`.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker obtains a session signer's signature over a payload where the signer intended permission 0 for call 0 and permission 1 for call 1. 2) Attacker reorders or duplicates calls so that permission 0 (which may be more permissive) is applied to a call the signer did not intend. 3) Because the permission index is attacker-chosen and not bound to the call, the validation passes if the permission's target matches. 4) The call executes with broader authority than the signer intended.
hypotheses.impact: Session signer's authority can be applied to unintended calls, enabling unauthorized transfers within the session's permission scope.
hypotheses.recommendation: Bind each permission index to a specific call index (e.g. include the call index in the signed hash) or require the permission index to equal the call index.

hypotheses.title: Read-only reentrancy in SessionManager.recoverSapientSignature via getLimitUsage
hypotheses.description: `recoverSapientSignature` is a `view` function that reads `getLimitUsage(wallet, usageHash)` from `PermissionValidator` storage to compute the cumulative usage for the current payload. Because it is a view function it can be called at any point during a transaction, including from within a callback (ERC-777/1155/721 hook, or a malicious target contract invoked by `Calls._execute`). The actual usage-limit increment is only written by the first call in the payload (`incrementUsageLimit`), which executes AFTER signature validation. Therefore, during the window between signature validation and the increment call, `getLimitUsage` returns the stale (pre-increment) value, and any contract that reads it (e.g., a DeFi protocol using the wallet's session limits as a trust signal) will see an inflated remaining allowance.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deploys a malicious target contract that, when called by the wallet, invokes `SessionManager.recoverSapientSignature` (or reads `getLimitUsage` directly) on the wallet. 2) The attacker submits a payload whose first call is `incrementUsageLimit` (required) and whose second call targets the malicious contract. 3) During the second call, the malicious contract reads `getLimitUsage` and observes the pre-increment value, then uses that stale value to authorize an action (e.g., a lending protocol that trusts the wallet's session limit). 4) The increment call then executes, but the damage is already done.
hypotheses.impact: External protocols that rely on the wallet's session usage limits as a trust signal can be tricked into over-extending credit or allowing over-spending, leading to loss of funds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Apply the usage-limit increment BEFORE any external call in the payload, or expose a non-view "effective limit" that accounts for pending increments.

hypotheses.title: SessionManager.recoverSapientSignature O(n^2) scan over sessionUsageLimits
hypotheses.description: For each explicit call, the code linearly scans `sessionUsageLimits` to find the matching signer, and `_validateExplicitCall` also linearly scans `allSessionPermissions` for the signer. With a payload containing many calls and many distinct session signers, the total work is O(calls × signers), and the payload size is attacker-controlled (bounded only by calldata/gas). A large payload can be crafted to consume all gas during signature validation, making the wallet unable to validate legitimate transactions that share the same nonce space.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker crafts a payload with many calls, each signed by a distinct session signer (or many calls with the same signer but forcing repeated scans). 2) Attacker submits `execute(payload, signature)` to the wallet. 3) Validation loops over calls and, for each, scans the growing `sessionUsageLimits`/`sessionPermissions` arrays. 4) Gas is exhausted inside validation, reverting the transaction.
hypotheses.impact: Legitimate transactions for the wallet can be blocked if the attacker can front-run or if the wallet's nonce space is shared; more generally, the wallet's session validation is vulnerable to gas-griefing with large payloads.
hypotheses.recommendation: Index session permissions and usage limits by signer (e.g. mapping or sorted structure) to make lookups O(1) or O(log n), and cap the number of distinct signers per payload.

hypotheses.title: Hooks fallback delegatecalls arbitrary hook without reentrancy guard
hypotheses.description: The fallback reads a hook implementation from storage keyed by `bytes4(msg.data)` and delegatecalls it. Hooks are added via `addHook` which is `onlySelf`, so only the wallet itself can add hooks. However, once a hook is added, any external caller can invoke the fallback with matching selector, causing the wallet to delegatecall into the hook implementation. The hook runs in the wallet's storage context and can modify any storage slot, including the implementation pointer, nonce, image hash, and reentrancy status. There is no reentrancy guard on the fallback, and no restriction on what the hook can do.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) A hook is added (legitimately, e.g. by the wallet owner via a signed payload). 2) Attacker calls the wallet's fallback with the hook's selector and crafted calldata. 3) The hook delegatecalls into the implementation, which can write to arbitrary storage (e.g. overwrite the implementation pointer to a malicious contract, or reset the reentrancy guard). 4) Attacker then exploits the modified state.
hypotheses.impact: Full wallet takeover if a hook is malicious or has a vulnerability; storage collision / arbitrary storage writes.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add a reentrancy guard to the fallback, restrict which storage slots hooks can write, or require hooks to be called only via the wallet's own execution flow.

hypotheses.title: Recovery.queuePayload allows anyone to queue payloads for any wallet/signer
hypotheses.description: `queuePayload` is external and permissionless: any caller can queue a payload for any `_wallet` and `_signer` as long as they provide a valid signature from `_signer` over the recovery payload. There is no check that `msg.sender` is the wallet or an authorized party. An attacker who obtains a valid signature (e.g. from a leaked or reused signature, or from a signer who signs a payload for a different purpose) can queue it, and the `AlreadyQueued` check prevents re-queuing the same payload but does not prevent queuing many distinct payloads. Combined with the unbounded array, this enables griefing.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker obtains a valid signature from `_signer` over a recovery payload (e.g. via phishing, signature reuse, or a compromised signer). 2) Attacker calls `queuePayload(_wallet, _signer, payload, sig)`. 3) The payload is queued and the timestamp is set. 4) Attacker repeats with many distinct payloads to bloat the queue.
hypotheses.impact: Queue bloat, potential unauthorized recovery initiation, and DoS of the recovery flow.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict `queuePayload` to `msg.sender == _wallet` or require an explicit authorization from the wallet, and bound the queue size.

hypotheses.title: Recover: same signature replayable on every wallet sharing imageHash (domain may omit wallet)
hypotheses.description: `Payload.hash()` uses `address(this)` as the verifyingContract, but `Payload.toEIP712` computes the struct hash using `parentWallets` (which is attacker-controlled in certain flows). For the sapient path, `BaseAuth.recoverSapientSignature` copies caller-supplied `_payload.parentWallets` into a fresh array and appends `msg.sender`, then `signatureValidation` recomputes the hash with those wallets. Since parentWallets come straight from calldata, an attacker can alter the wallets list to match the one used by a signature intended for a *different* parent context. Additionally, the EIP-712 domain uses `_decoded.noChainId` (attacker-controlled), so a signature made for chain A can be reused on chain B by flipping the noChainId bit if the original signature included noChainId, or by simply signing with noChainId=true.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes a sapient signature for a legitimate wallet context with a particular `parentWallets` array. 2) Crafts a new payload with the same struct hash but pointing conveniently. 3) Replays. Or flips `noChainId` and reuses on another chain.
hypotheses.impact: Cross-chain and cross-context replay of wallet-authorizing signatures.
hypotheses.recommendation: Include `block.chainid` unconditionally in the domain separator (or force noChainId=false in sapient recover), and don't trust caller-supplied parentWallets for hash computation.

hypotheses.title: Static signature can be set with arbitrary future timestamp by wallet itself
hypotheses.description: `setStaticSignature` is `onlySelf`, so it must be invoked via the wallet's own execution path. However, `signatureValidation` treats a static signature as valid whenever `timestamp > block.timestamp` and `addr == address(0)` (i.e., no caller restriction). This means a wallet can set a static signature with `_address = address(0)` and a far-future `_timestamp`, which makes any caller able to execute the payload matching `_hash` without any signature. Combined with the fact that `_hash` is the payload hash (which includes nonce/space), this is a pre-authorization mechanism. The economic flaw is that a session signer or any party who can get the wallet to self-execute a `setStaticSignature` call can pre-authorize arbitrary future payloads, bypassing the normal signature threshold and session limits entirely.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker obtains a session signature that permits a call to `setStaticSignature` (or any call that the wallet will self-execute). 2) Attacker crafts a payload that calls `setStaticSignature(hashOfTargetPayload, address(0), farFutureTimestamp)`. 3) The wallet self-executes this, storing the static signature. 4) Attacker later submits the target payload with the static-signature flag set; `signatureValidation` returns `true` because `addr == address(0)` and the timestamp is in the future, bypassing all threshold/session checks.
hypotheses.impact: Session limits and signature thresholds can be bypassed, allowing unauthorized execution of arbitrary calls from the wallet, including draining funds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require `_address != address(0)` in `setStaticSignature`, or restrict static signatures to a specific caller, and/or bound the timestamp to a reasonable maximum.

hypotheses.title: SessionManager.recoverSapientSignature trusts msg.sender as wallet
hypotheses.description: The function sets `address wallet = msg.sender` and uses it for all usage-limit accounting (getLimitUsage, _validateExplicitCall, _validateLimitUsageIncrement). It assumes the caller is the wallet, but any contract can call `recoverSapientSignature` on the SessionManager (e.g. via BaseSig FLAG_SIGNATURE_SAPIENT, where the wallet is the caller of the sapient signer). If a wallet's signature tree includes a SessionManager sapient node, the SessionManager is invoked with `msg.sender` being the wallet, which is correct — but the same SessionManager instance is shared across all wallets, and the wallet address is derived purely from msg.sender without verifying that msg.sender actually is a wallet that has this SessionManager configured. An attacker who can get a wallet to call into SessionManager (e.g. by crafting a payload whose signature tree references SessionManager as a sapient signer) can cause usage limits to be tracked against an arbitrary address.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker crafts a payload whose signature tree contains a FLAG_SIGNATURE_SAPIENT node pointing at SessionManager. 2) Attacker gets a victim wallet to validate this signature (e.g. via ERC-4337 validateUserOp or execute). 3) SessionManager.recoverSapientSignature is called with msg.sender = victim wallet. 4) SessionManager reads/writes usage limits keyed by victim wallet, but the session permissions and signers are attacker-controlled. 5) Attacker can consume or reset the victim's usage limits, or bypass limits by using a fresh wallet address as msg.sender.
hypotheses.impact: Bypass of session usage limits; incorrect accounting of value/usage limits; potential unauthorized spending up to the session's valueLimit.
hypotheses.recommendation: Derive the wallet address from the payload context (e.g. pass it explicitly or use the parentWallets mechanism) rather than trusting msg.sender, and verify msg.sender is a legitimate wallet.

hypotheses.title: Simulator.simulate reads uninitialized behaviorOnError and can revert whole simulation for any caller
hypotheses.description: `simulate` is fully open and returns results only for the caller's own transaction, so an attacker cannot persist any state through it — but combined with the missing access control the same open entry point lets any caller make `Simulator` (a `Stage2Module` shared by wallets in the architecture) perform arbitrary reads and calls that return data into the caller's context. Because it repeatedly invokes attacker-controlled target contracts via `LibOptim.call`, any target can observe `msg.sender == Simulator` and misbehave (e.g., treat simulator calls as privileged). The issue is reachability of untrusted targets via a contract address that some integrations may treat as authority.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) A protocol whitelists `Simulator` as a trusted module address. 2) Attacker calls `Simulator.simulate` with a call targeting that protocol. 3) The protocol sees `msg.sender == Simulator` and executes privileged logic.
hypotheses.impact: Any integration that trusts the Simulator's address as an authority becomes exploitable; storage corruption if targets delegatecall back into Simulator.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict `simulate` to a caller-supplied whitelist, require `nonReentrant`, and document that no external integration should grant the Simulator any trust.

hypotheses.title: First-depositor / donation attack on wallet via create2 salt
hypotheses.description: The wallet is deployed via `create2` using `_salt` as the imageHash. The wallet address is deterministic based on the imageHash. An attacker can pre-compute the wallet address for a known imageHash and send native tokens or ERC20 tokens to that address before deployment. When the legitimate user deploys the wallet, the pre-sent funds are already in the wallet. While this is not a direct theft (the wallet is controlled by the imageHash signers), it can cause accounting confusion if the wallet's logic assumes a zero starting balance. More critically, if the wallet is used as a session manager or has value-tracking logic, the pre-sent funds could be counted as part of the wallet's holdings, potentially affecting value limits or other accounting.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker computes the wallet address for a target imageHash. 2) Attacker sends tokens to that address. 3) Legitimate user deploys the wallet. 4) The wallet now has a non-zero balance that was not intended. 5) If the wallet's session logic or value tracking assumes a zero starting balance, the attacker's donation could be used to manipulate limits or cause unexpected behavior.
hypotheses.impact: Potential accounting confusion; attacker can influence the wallet's initial balance, which may affect value limits or other balance-dependent logic.
hypotheses.recommendation: Document that wallets should not assume a zero starting balance; consider initializing balance-dependent state explicitly on deployment.

hypotheses.title: Rounding in Base64 encoding may cause signature verification mismatch
hypotheses.description: The `encode` function uses `shl(2, div(add(dataLength, 2), 3))` to compute the encoded length. This is a ceiling division, which is correct for base64. However, the padding logic uses `div(2, mod(dataLength, 3))` to determine the offset `o`. For `dataLength % 3 == 0`, `o = 0`; for `1`, `o = 2`; for `2`, `o = 1`. This is correct. The issue is that the function does not validate that the input `data` is properly padded or that the output is correctly formatted for all edge cases, particularly when `dataLength` is very large or when the input contains specific byte patterns. In the context of WebAuthn, the challenge is base64-encoded and compared against the clientDataJSON. If the encoding is incorrect for certain inputs, the signature verification will fail, potentially locking out legitimate users.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) A legitimate user attempts to sign a transaction using WebAuthn. 2) The challenge is base64-encoded using this function. 3) If the encoding produces an incorrect result for the specific challenge (e.g., due to an edge case in the padding logic), the signature verification fails. 4) The user is unable to execute transactions, effectively locking their funds.
hypotheses.impact: Legitimate users may be unable to execute transactions if the base64 encoding produces incorrect results for certain challenges, leading to a denial of service.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add comprehensive tests for the base64 encoding function across all possible input lengths and byte patterns; consider using a well-audited library.

hypotheses.title: Cumulative usage limit can be reset by omitting prior calls in payload
hypotheses.description: For cumulative rules, the code looks up `previousUsage` from the in-memory `newUsageLimits` array first, and only falls back to `getLimitUsage(wallet, usageHash)` (storage) if `previousUsage == 0`. If a prior call in the same payload already accumulated usage and stored it in `newUsageLimits`, a later call with the same `usageHash` will read that value. However, if the attacker crafts a payload where the cumulative call is the first (and only) call using that `usageHash`, `previousUsage` is read from storage — which is only updated by the `incrementUsageLimit` call at index 0. If the attacker omits or manipulates the increment call, the storage value may be stale or zero, allowing the cumulative limit to be bypassed.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes that cumulative usage is tracked in storage via `incrementUsageLimit`. 2) Attacker crafts a payload where the cumulative call is executed but the required `incrementUsageLimit` call at index 0 is either absent (if no limits are used) or contains manipulated values. 3) `_validateLimitUsageIncrement` checks that the first call matches the expected increment data, but the expected data is derived from the in-memory `sessionUsageLimits` which the attacker influences via the payload. 4) If the attacker can make `sessionUsageLimits` empty or zero, the increment check is skipped and storage is never updated, so cumulative limits reset.
hypotheses.impact: Session usage limits (e.g. spending caps) can be bypassed, allowing unlimited spending within a session.
hypotheses.recommendation: Always read the authoritative cumulative usage from storage and require the increment call to be present and correct whenever any cumulative rule is used.

hypotheses.title: Front-running queuePayload to grief recovery via AlreadyQueued
hypotheses.description: `queuePayload` is permissionless and reverts with `AlreadyQueued` if `timestampForQueuedPayload[_wallet][_signer][payloadHash] != 0`. An attacker who observes a pending recovery transaction in the mempool can front-run it by calling `queuePayload` with the same `_wallet`, `_signer`, `_payload`, and `_signature` (all of which are visible in the pending tx). This sets the timestamp to the attacker's block timestamp, which is EARLIER than the victim's intended timestamp. The victim's transaction then reverts with `AlreadyQueued`. The attacker has effectively reset the recovery clock to an earlier time, which is actually beneficial to the victim (earlier timestamp means the delta-time requirement is satisfied sooner), so this is a griefing vector only if the attacker can also prevent the victim from re-queuing — but since the timestamp is already set, the victim cannot re-queue and must wait for the delta time from the attacker's timestamp.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Victim submits `queuePayload(wallet, signer, payload, sig)` to the mempool. 2) Attacker sees the tx, copies the exact calldata, and submits the same call with higher gas. 3) Attacker's tx executes first, setting `timestampForQueuedPayload` to the attacker's block timestamp. 4) Victim's tx reverts with `AlreadyQueued`. 5) The recovery is now gated on the attacker's timestamp, which the attacker can manipulate by choosing when to submit (e.g., delaying until a favorable block).
hypotheses.impact: Recovery timing can be manipulated by an untrusted actor; if the attacker front-runs with a very early timestamp, the recovery becomes executable sooner than the victim intended, potentially allowing a compromised signer to recover the wallet before the victim can react.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require `msg.sender` to be the `_signer` or the `_wallet`, or allow re-queuing to update the timestamp if the caller is authorized.

hypotheses.title: Static signature replay across chains via noChainId flag
hypotheses.description: When the static signature path is taken (`signatureFlag & 0x80 == 0x80`), the code computes `opHash = _payload.hash()` and looks up `_getStaticSignature(opHash)`. The `_payload.hash()` uses `domainSeparator(_decoded.noChainId, address(this))`, and `noChainId` is set from the signature flag in `BaseSig.recover` (bit 0x02). However, in the static-signature branch, `noChainId` is never set from the signature — it defaults to `false` (the default for a fresh `Payload.Decoded`), so the chainId IS included. But the static signature is keyed only by `opHash`, and `opHash` is computed from the payload which includes `noChainId`. If an attacker can craft a payload with `noChainId = true` (via the non-static path) and get a static signature set for that hash, the same static signature could be replayed on a different chain where the same `opHash` is produced. More directly: the static signature is stored per-hash and has no chain binding beyond what's in the hash, and the hash's chain binding depends on `noChainId` which is attacker-controllable in the non-static path.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker obtains a static signature for a payload on chain A (e.g., via a legitimate flow). 2) Attacker replays the same payload on chain B. 3) If the payload's `noChainId` flag is set, the `opHash` is identical on both chains, so the static signature is valid on chain B. 4) The attacker executes the payload on chain B without authorization.
hypotheses.impact: Cross-chain replay of authorized operations; loss of funds on the target chain.
hypotheses.recommendation: Include `block.chainid` in the static signature key unconditionally, or reject `noChainId` payloads when using static signatures.

hypotheses.title: Calls._execute reverts on NotEnoughGas, blocking remaining calls
hypotheses.description: When a call specifies a `gasLimit` and `gasleft() < gasLimit`, `_execute` reverts with `NotEnoughGas` instead of skipping or aborting that call. Because the entire payload is atomic, a single call with an over-large gas limit (or a call that consumes gas earlier in the sequence) causes the whole transaction to revert, even if subsequent calls would have succeeded. An attacker who can influence the payload (e.g. via a session signer or a compromised signer) can craft a payload that always reverts, blocking execution of otherwise valid calls.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker (or a session signer with limited permissions) crafts a payload where an early call has a `gasLimit` larger than the remaining gas. 2) Attacker submits the payload. 3) `_execute` reverts at the `NotEnoughGas` check, aborting the entire batch. 4) Any intended later calls (e.g. withdrawals) never execute.
hypotheses.impact: Batched operations that include a gas-heavy call can be permanently blocked; if the payload is the only path to move funds, funds can be stuck.
hypotheses.recommendation: Treat `NotEnoughGas` as a per-call failure governed by `behaviorOnError` (ignore/abort) rather than an unconditional revert, or validate gas limits before committing to the batch.

hypotheses.title: WebAuthn challenge comparison permits unbounded trailing challenge data
hypotheses.description: The comparison checks `keccak256(add(o, c), q) == keccak256(add(encoded, 0x13), q)` where `q = encoded.length + 0x0d`. Because `q` is derived from the base64-encoded challenge length, the check only covers the encoded challenge bytes; the surrounding `"challenge":"` prefix is checked byte-by-byte, and a closing `"` is required. But there is no check that `challengeIndex` corresponds to a *complete* `"challenge":"..."` occurrence without allowing `typeIndex` to overlap the challenge region in a way that lets a longer JS string satisfy both fields with different meaning. Additionally, the challenge is `abi.encodePacked(_digest)` where `_digest` is 32 bytes and gets base64-encoded; an attacker can craft `clientDataJSON` where the challenge region contains the digest bytes followed by extra valid characters before the closing quote, since `keccak256` is over exactly `q` bytes equal to the length of the encoded challenge + `"challenge":"` prefix — this only works if the extra bytes equal what base64 of the encoded challenge would be, which they must to match the hash. The actual weakness is that `clientDataJSON` is attacker-supplied and `challengeIndex` is attacker-supplied, and the code does not verify that `challengeIndex` falls inside `clientDataJSON`'s length (only a pressed inequality with overflow protection). A crafted `clientDataJSON` with a `"challenge":"..."` matching the digest can be replayed for the same digest across contexts because there is no binding to origin/RP.
hypotheses.attackPath: N/A — the concrete exploit requires a deeper out-of-bounds read, but the origin/RP binding is intentionally omitted and any attacker who intercepts a valid WebAuthn signature for a given digest can replay it against any wallet whose passkey root matches.
hypotheses.impact: Replay of passkey-authorized operations if the same digest occurs.
hypotheses.recommendation: Bind the challenge to an anti-replay nonce (already via opHash) and verify the challengeIndex is within clientDataJSON boundaries explicitly.

hypotheses.title: SessionSig identity signature does not bind to session config / blacklist
hypotheses.description: The identity signature is computed over `att.toHash()` (Attestation contents only). The imageHash (derived from session configuration: permissions, blacklist, identity signer) is not covered by any signature — it's just used to look up the wallet's stored imageHash. This means an attestation can be reused across any wallet that has the *same identity signer* configured, even if their session configuration (permissions/deadline/blacklist) differs. Combined with the fact that `recoverSapientSignature` only checks `sig.imageHash` matches the wallet — which is derived from attacker-supplied session config bytes — an attacker who reuses a valid attestation can produce a session config containing permissions the identity signer never approved, as long as the wallet's actual configured imageHash happens to match (which the attacker must know, but imageHash is public via `imageHash()`). So config is unauthenticated.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker learns wallet's configured imageHash (public). 2) Constructs session config whose merkle tree hashes to that imageHash — but this requires preimage of the wallet's chosen config, which the attacker doesn't know all fields of. However the identity-signer leaves the config free to any massaged set, permitting swapping permission arrays as long as the root matches.
hypotheses.impact: Identity signer may be tricked into approving attestations that are reused with different permissions than intended.
hypotheses.recommendation: Include the wallet address and a versioned configuration commitment inside the attestation hash, and require the identity signer's signature to cover the session configuration root.

hypotheses.title: onlyFallback error flag reset allows skipping fallback calls
hypotheses.description: The `errorFlag` is reset to `false` at the start of each iteration (after the `onlyFallback` check). This means `onlyFallback` calls only trigger if the *immediately preceding* call failed. If a call fails with `BEHAVIOR_IGNORE_ERROR`, `errorFlag` is set to `true`, but then the next iteration resets it to `false` before checking `onlyFallback`. Wait — the check happens before the reset, so the fallback call does execute. However, if the fallback call itself fails with `BEHAVIOR_IGNORE_ERROR`, `errorFlag` is set to `true` again, and the next `onlyFallback` call will also execute. This chaining is intended. The economic concern is that a session signer can craft a payload where a benign call fails (e.g., a call to a contract that always reverts) to trigger a fallback call that performs a privileged action, and the session validation in `SessionManager` bans `BEHAVIOR_ABORT_ON_ERROR` but not `BEHAVIOR_IGNORE_ERROR` combined with `onlyFallback`. This allows a session signer to execute calls that were not intended to be permitted by the session's permissions, because the fallback call's permission is validated against the same `permissionIdx` but the fallback semantics may not be accounted for.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Session signer crafts a payload with call[0] = a call that always reverts with `BEHAVIOR_IGNORE_ERROR`, and call[1] = a privileged call with `onlyFallback = true`. 2) Session validation checks each call's permission independently, but the fallback call's permission may be satisfied by a permission intended for a different call, or the fallback semantics allow executing a call that would otherwise be blocked. 3) The fallback call executes, performing an action the session owner did not intend to authorize.
hypotheses.impact: Session permissions can be bypassed via fallback call semantics, allowing a session signer to execute unauthorized calls.
hypotheses.recommendation: In `SessionManager.recoverSapientSignature`, reject `onlyFallback` calls or validate that fallback calls have their own explicit permissions.

hypotheses.title: Cumulative usage limit can be bypassed by splitting across multiple calls
hypotheses.description: For cumulative rules, `previousUsage` is read from `newUsageLimits` (in-memory, per-payload) first, and only falls back to storage if `previousUsage == 0`. If a cumulative rule's usage is legitimately 0 (e.g., the first use), the code falls back to `getLimitUsage(wallet, usageHash)` which is also 0, so no issue. However, if the in-memory `usageLimit.usageAmount` is 0 because the rule was just initialized in this payload, `previousUsage` is 0 and the code reads storage — which is correct. The real issue: `newUsageLimits` is only persisted to storage via the `incrementUsageLimit` call, which is validated by `_validateLimitUsageIncrement` against the payload's computed limits. If a session signer crafts a payload where the cumulative usage is computed but the `incrementUsageLimit` call is omitted or manipulated, the storage is not updated, and the next payload starts from the old storage value. But `_validateLimitUsageIncrement` requires the increment call if `sessionUsageLimits.length > 0`. The bypass: if the attacker can make `sessionUsageLimits` empty (e.g., by using a non-cumulative permission), the increment call is not required, and cumulative usage is never persisted. This is by design for non-cumulative rules, but a cumulative rule with `usageAmount` that happens to be 0 in the payload would not trigger the increment requirement.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Session signer uses a cumulative rule where the extracted value is 0 (e.g., a parameter that is 0). 2) `validatePermission` computes `value256 = 0 + previousUsage`, and if `previousUsage` is 0, `usageLimit.usageAmount = 0`. 3) The `sessionUsageLimits` array may still include this limit (since `limits.length > 0`), so the increment call is required. However, if the attacker can structure the payload so that the cumulative rule's usage is not tracked (e.g., by using a different permission index), the storage is not updated, and the cumulative cap is never enforced across payloads.
hypotheses.impact: Cumulative spending limits can be bypassed across multiple payloads, allowing a session signer to spend beyond the intended cap.
hypotheses.recommendation: Ensure that any cumulative rule always results in a non-zero `usageAmount` being persisted, or track cumulative usage separately from the value (e.g., always increment a counter).

hypotheses.title: SessionManager MAX_SPACE off-by-one allows space == type(uint80).max
hypotheses.description: `MAX_SPACE = type(uint80).max - 1` and the check is `if (payload.space > MAX_SPACE) revert`. This means `payload.space == type(uint80).max` is rejected, but `payload.space == type(uint80).max - 1` is allowed. The comment says "This excludes half the possible bits (uint160 vs uint80)" — the intent appears to be to exclude the upper half of the uint160 space, i.e. reject space >= 2^80. With MAX_SPACE = 2^80 - 2, the value 2^80 - 1 is allowed, which is still in the upper half. The boundary is off by one relative to the stated intent.
hypotheses.attackPath: A session signer can use space = 2^80 - 1, which the code intends to forbid (upper half of uint160 space reserved for non-session use). This may collide with nonce spaces used by other modules or allow sessions to consume nonces in a reserved range.
hypotheses.impact: Nonce space collision between session and non-session usage; potential replay or nonce confusion across modules.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use `MAX_SPACE = type(uint80).max` (i.e. 2^80 - 1) and reject `space > MAX_SPACE`, or explicitly reject `space >= 2^80`.

hypotheses.title: Calls._execute delegatecall passes _startingGas from outer frame, enabling gas griefing
hypotheses.description: When `call.delegateCall` is true, the code forwards `_startingGas` (the gas at the start of the outer `execute` call) to `handleSequenceDelegateCall`. The delegated extension receives the outer frame's starting gas, not the current gas. A malicious or buggy delegated extension can use this to compute gas refunds or limits incorrectly, or to consume all remaining gas. More importantly, the `gasLimit` check `gasleft() < gasLimit` is done before the call, but the delegatecall is given `gasLimit == 0 ? gasleft() : gasLimit` — if gasLimit is 0, the entire remaining gas is forwarded, which combined with the 63/64 rule can cause the outer call to run out of gas unexpectedly.
hypotheses.attackPath: A malicious delegated extension (registered via a hook or via the wallet's own config) can be invoked with delegatecall and consume all gas, or use `_startingGas` to misreport. Since delegatecall runs in the wallet's context, a malicious extension can also directly manipulate storage.
hypotheses.impact: Gas griefing; potential for a delegated extension to drain the wallet's gas or manipulate state.
hypotheses.recommendation: Pass the current `gasleft()` rather than `_startingGas` to the delegated extension, or document and constrain the extension's use of this value.

hypotheses.title: BaseAuth.signatureValidation static signature check uses msg.sender without binding to wallet
hypotheses.description: When the static signature flag is set, the code checks `if (addr != address(0) && addr != msg.sender) revert InvalidStaticSignatureWrongCaller`. The static signature is stored per-wallet (in the wallet's own storage), so `msg.sender` here is whoever called the wallet's `execute`/`isValidSignature`. For ERC-4337, `msg.sender` is the EntryPoint, not the user. For direct `execute` calls, `msg.sender` is the caller. This means a static signature set for a specific caller (e.g. a relayer) can be used by anyone who can make the wallet call `signatureValidation` with that caller as msg.sender — but more critically, if `addr == address(0)`, the check is skipped entirely, allowing any caller to use the static signature.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) A static signature is set with `_address = address(0)` (e.g. to allow any caller). 2) Any external actor can call the wallet's `execute` with the static signature flag and the matching opHash. 3) The signature is accepted regardless of caller. If the static signature was intended to be caller-restricted, this bypasses it.
hypotheses.impact: Unauthorized execution if a static signature is set with address(0) or if the caller check is bypassed via a different entry point.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require `addr != address(0)` when the static signature is used, or bind the static signature to the wallet address rather than msg.sender.
